Barnard and Rubin's Small-Sample Degrees of Freedom for Multiple Imputation

Source: R/df_barnard_rubin.R
df_barnard_rubin.Rd

Computes the degrees of freedom of the t reference distribution for an estimate pooled over m imputed data sets by Rubin's (1987) rules, using Barnard and Rubin's (1999) small-sample formula, together with the quantities it is built from: the total variance, the fraction of missing information the imputations estimate, the relative increase in variance due to the missing values, and the two components of the degrees of freedom. The function is vectorized over parameters.

Usage

df_barnard_rubin(between, within, m, df_complete = Inf, floor = 3)

Arguments

between

The between-imputation variance \(B\) of each parameter: the variance, with divisor \(m - 1\), of its m estimates. A numeric vector, one value per parameter, whose names label the rows. (It is not called B because DMAR keeps B for the number of bootstrap replications.)

within

The within-imputation variance \(\bar{U}\) of each parameter: the mean of its m squared standard errors. A numeric vector of the same length as between.

m

The number of imputations, a single whole number of 2 or more.

df_complete

The complete data degrees of freedom, of length 1 or the length of between. Defaults to Inf, which gives Rubin's (1987) large-sample degrees of freedom; a small-sample analysis should supply its complete data error degrees of freedom.

floor

The lower bound on the degrees of freedom: a single number of 0 or more. Defaults to 3, von Hippel's (2016) recommendation; 0 reproduces Barnard and Rubin (1999).

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with one row per parameter and the columns term, df (bounded below by floor), df_unbounded (\(\nu_{BR}\)), gamma, relative_increase (\(r\)), total_variance (\(T\)), nu_m, nu_obs, and at_floor. The attributes m, df_complete, and floor record the call, and the printed table, at the console or knitted, is followed by a line naming the rule, m, df_complete, and the floor. A missing input value gives missing values in its row.

Details

Rubin's rules. Each of the m completed data sets gives an estimate \(\hat{\theta}_d\) and a squared standard error \(U_d\). The pooled estimate \(\bar{\theta}\) is their mean, the within-imputation variance is \(\bar{U} = m^{-1} \sum_d U_d\), the between-imputation variance is \(B = (m - 1)^{-1} \sum_d (\hat{\theta}_d - \bar{\theta})^2\), and the total variance of the pooled estimate is $$T = \bar{U} + (1 + 1/m) B.$$ The share of the total variance due to the missing values, $$\gamma = (1 + 1/m) B / T,$$ is the multiple imputation estimate of the fraction of missing information, which mice reports as lambda, and \(r = (1 + 1/m) B / \bar{U}\) is the relative increase in variance due to nonresponse (mice's riv). mice's fmi column is a different quantity, \((r + 2/(\nu + 3))/(r + 1)\), which adjusts \(\gamma\) for the degrees of freedom. Von Hippel's (2016) Eq. 25 prints the within-imputation variance in place of \(B\) in the numerator of \(\gamma\), a typographical error: that ratio would exceed 1 with no missing values at all.

The degrees of freedom. Rubin's (1987) degrees of freedom, $$\nu_m = (m - 1) / \gamma^2,$$ reflect only the finite number of imputations: they treat each completed data analysis as if it had infinitely many degrees of freedom, and when \(\gamma\) is small they can exceed the degrees of freedom the analysis would have with no missing values at all, which cannot be right in a small sample. Barnard and Rubin (1999) combine them with observed data degrees of freedom, $$\nu_{obs} = \nu_{com} (1 - \gamma) \frac{\nu_{com} + 1}{\nu_{com} + 3},$$ where \(\nu_{com}\), given as df_complete, is the complete data degrees of freedom (for a regression coefficient, \(n - k\), with \(k\) the number of regression parameters), as $$\nu_{BR} = \left(\frac{1}{\nu_m} + \frac{1}{\nu_{obs}}\right)^{-1},$$ which never exceeds \(\nu_{obs}\) and hence never exceeds \(\nu_{com}\). The formulas are as von Hippel (2016, Eqs. 23 and 24) writes them, and they agree with mice's barnard.rubin(). With df_complete = Inf, the default, \(\nu_{obs}\) is infinite and \(\nu_{BR}\) is Rubin's \(\nu_m\). The observed data degrees of freedom are df_missing's "complete_df" rule, and von Hippel's degrees of freedom for maximum likelihood are the limit of \(\nu_{BR}\) as the number of imputations grows, where \(\nu_m\) becomes infinite.

The floor. An estimate of \(\gamma\) near 1 drives the degrees of freedom toward 0, where the t quantile grows without bound. In von Hippel's (2016, p. 431) simulation of 25 cases with half the values of one variable missing at random, 24% of the Barnard and Rubin degrees of freedom were below 3, 11% below 2, and 2% below 1, and some intervals were orders of magnitude longer than coverage required. He bounds the degrees of freedom below at 3 (his Eq. 27), which is the default floor = 3 here; floor = 0 reproduces Barnard and Rubin's formula, and mice, exactly. The unbounded value is kept in df_unbounded, and at_floor marks the rows where the bound applied.

DMAR does not impute; this function serves analyses pooled elsewhere and the comparison of maximum likelihood with multiple imputation. For a FIML fit, df_missing gives the corresponding degrees of freedom from the fit's own fraction of missing information, without imputations.

References

Barnard, J., & Rubin, D. B. (1999). Small-sample degrees of freedom with multiple imputation. Biometrika, 86(4), 948–955. doi:10.1093/biomet/86.4.948

Rubin, D. B. (1987). Multiple imputation for nonresponse in surveys. Wiley.

van Buuren, S., & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, K. (2011). mice: Multivariate imputation by chained equations in R. Journal of Statistical Software, 45(3), 1–67. doi:10.18637/jss.v045.i03

von Hippel, P. T. (2016). New confidence intervals and bias comparisons show that maximum likelihood can beat multiple imputation in small samples. Structural Equation Modeling, 23(3), 422–437. doi:10.1080/10705511.2015.1047931

See also

df_missing for the degrees of freedom of a FIML estimate.

Other missing data: cov_fiml(), df_missing(), fraction_missing_information(), missing_coverage(), missing_patterns()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# One coefficient from m = 5 imputations, with complete data error
# degrees of freedom of 23: B = 0.04 and a within-imputation variance of
# 0.10. floor = 0 gives Barnard and Rubin's formula itself.
df_barnard_rubin(between = 0.04, within = 0.10, m = 5, df_complete = 23,
                 floor = 0)
#>  term        df     df_unbounded gamma relative_increase total_variance nu_m  
#>  parameter_1 10.416 10.416       0.324 0.480             0.148          38.028
#>  nu_obs at_floor
#>  14.345 FALSE   
#> 
#> Degrees of freedom: Barnard and Rubin's (1999) rule for m = 5 imputations,
#> 1 / (1 / nu_m + 1 / nu_obs) with df_complete = 23, bounded below at 0

# Rubin's (1987) large-sample degrees of freedom are 38, well above the
# 23 a complete data analysis of these cases would have.
df_barnard_rubin(between = 0.04, within = 0.10, m = 5)
#>  term        df     df_unbounded gamma relative_increase total_variance nu_m  
#>  parameter_1 38.028 38.028       0.324 0.480             0.148          38.028
#>  nu_obs at_floor
#>  Inf    FALSE   
#> 
#> Degrees of freedom: Rubin's (1987) large-sample rule for m = 5 imputations,
#> (m - 1) / gamma^2 (df_complete = Inf), bounded below at 3

# Pooling by hand: five estimates of each of two coefficients and their
# squared standard errors (illustrative values), one column per
# coefficient.
est <- cbind(slope = c(0.42, 0.51, 0.38, 0.47, 0.55),
             intercept = c(1.90, 1.94, 1.88, 1.93, 1.91))
u <- cbind(slope = c(0.010, 0.011, 0.009, 0.010, 0.012),
           intercept = c(0.020, 0.021, 0.019, 0.020, 0.022))
df_barnard_rubin(between = apply(est, 2, var), within = colMeans(u),
                 m = 5, df_complete = 23)
#>  term      df     df_unbounded gamma relative_increase total_variance nu_m    
#>  slope     9.749  9.749        0.348 0.534             0.016          32.990  
#>  intercept 20.432 20.432       0.032 0.034             0.021          3800.614
#>  nu_obs at_floor
#>  13.838 FALSE   
#>  20.542 FALSE   
#> 
#> Degrees of freedom: Barnard and Rubin's (1999) rule for m = 5 imputations,
#> 1 / (1 / nu_m + 1 / nu_obs) with df_complete = 23, bounded below at 3
